content.title: About
content.content: Garlic (Allium sativum) is a bulb vegetable native to Central Asia and a close relative of onions, leeks, and chives. Each bulb is made up of several cloves wrapped in papery skin. It has a pungent, savory aroma and flavor that mellows and sweetens when cooked. Garlic is used worldwide as a flavoring and has a long history in traditional medicine.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Garlic has been cultivated for more than 5,000 years.
When garlic is crushed or chopped, an enzyme reaction forms allicin, which gives it its sharp smell.
Letting chopped garlic rest for about ten minutes before cooking can help preserve its beneficial compounds.
Black garlic is whole garlic aged under controlled heat and humidity, giving it a sweet, soft texture.
Garlic is one of the most widely used seasonings in the world.

items.title: Contains sulfur compounds
items.content: Allicin and other organosulfur compounds in garlic are being studied for their biological activity.

items.title: Provides vitamin C and selenium
items.content: These support immune function and antioxidant defenses, though garlic is usually eaten in small amounts.

items.title: May support heart health
items.content: Some studies suggest that garlic may help improve certain cardiovascular markers, although more research is needed.

items.title: Adds flavor without salt
items.content: Garlic can add taste to food and reduce the need for added salt.

items.title: Breath and body odor
items.content: Garlic can cause strong breath and body odor.

items.title: Digestive discomfort
items.content: Garlic may cause heartburn, gas, or stomach upset in some people, especially raw.

items.title: Possible medication interactions
items.content: Large amounts or garlic supplements may affect blood clotting and interact with some medications. People taking blood thinners or planning surgery should consult a healthcare professional.

items.title: Garlic in oil
items.content: Garlic stored in oil at room temperature can grow the bacteria that cause botulism. Refrigerate garlic-in-oil mixtures and use them quickly.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Garlic can be minced, sliced, crushed, roasted whole, sautéed, or added to sauces, soups, marinades, dressings, and spreads. Raw garlic has the strongest flavor, while roasted garlic is mild and sweet. Add it near the end of sautéing so it does not burn and turn bitter.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store whole garlic bulbs in a cool, dry, dark, well-ventilated place, where they keep for weeks to months. Do not refrigerate whole bulbs for long, as this can cause sprouting. Peeled or chopped garlic should be refrigerated in an airtight container and used within a few days. Do not keep garlic in oil at room temperature.
